learningObjective: Compare HBM traffic patterns between naive attention (materialized S = QK^T) and FlashAttention (block-tiled, streamed).

canonicalClaims.claim: Naive attention that materializes S = QK^T in HBM has Ω(N^2) HBM traffic for S alone; FlashAttention keeps S on-chip and has HBM traffic O(N^2 d / M), where M is on-chip memory per SM, so its I/O falls below the naive baseline as N grows.
conditions: Baseline actually stores S in HBM (unfused softmax).
SMEM/register file M >= size of a Q-tile plus a K/V-tile.
nonImplications: Does not imply FLOP count changes; forward FLOPs remain O(N^2 d).
Does not imply that every 'naive' implementation writes S to HBM; some fuse it partially.

misconceptions.claim: FlashAttention increases HBM traffic; its benefit is register/SMEM economy.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The paper's central result is that HBM I/O is reduced, not increased.
Forward FLOPs are unchanged; backward FLOPs slightly increase due to recomputation.

misconceptions.claim: HBM traffic of naive attention scales as O(N d), the same as loading Q, K, V.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Naive attention writes and re-reads S of size N^2, which dominates I/O.

implementationFacts: Typical FA tile sizes: B_r = B_c = 128 on Ampere; larger on Hopper.
The Q loop is outer; each Q tile is loaded once per K/V pass, or vice versa depending on FA v1 vs v2 loop order.
performanceScenarios: For long context (N in tens of thousands), the O(N^2) S traffic saved by FA dominates any secondary cost.
